meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you are neutral in situations of injustice, you have chosen the side of the oppressor'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes — this one is really Tutu's. Documented by 1984 in Robert McAfee Brown's book Unexpected News (p. 19), and often confused with Elie Wiesel's Nobel line.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1931–2021 · South African archbishop, anti-apartheid leader & Nobel Peace laureate
answer.sourceLine: This is one of the rare feel-good justice lines the famous name really did say. It is documented in print by 1984: Robert McAfee Brown quotes Tutu with these exact words in Unexpected News: Reading the Bible with Third World Eyes (p. 19), and Wikiquote lists it in its Sourced section. Because Brown is quoting Tutu, the original occasion (a sermon or address during apartheid) isn’t separately pinned — but authorship is genuine and undisputed.

source.excerpt: If you are neutral in situations of injustice, you have chosen the side of the oppressor. If an elephant has its foot on the tail of a mouse and you say that you are neutral, the mouse will not appreciate your neutrality.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line in its Sourced section for Desmond Tutu, cited to Robert McAfee Brown’s Unexpected News (1984), p. 19.
The full passage — with the elephant standing on the mouse’s tail — appears at the front of Brown’s book, and the book itself is scanned on the Internet Archive.
A near-identical thought — that neutrality helps the oppressor — comes from Elie Wiesel’s 1986 Nobel acceptance speech, and the two lines are frequently mixed up; Tutu’s is the earlier (1984).
source.excerptNote: The neutrality line is almost always quoted on its own, but in Brown’s book it is paired with Tutu’s vivid elephant-and-mouse image, which makes the point concrete.

author.name: Desmond Tutu
author.heading: About Desmond Tutu
author.metaLine: 1931–2021 · South African archbishop, anti-apartheid leader & Nobel Peace laureate
author.bio: Desmond Mpilo Tutu was the Anglican Archbishop of Cape Town and one of the moral leaders of the struggle against apartheid, awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984. After majority rule he chaired South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission. His preaching leaned on vivid, homely images — the elephant and the mouse among them — which is part of why lines like this one travelled so far.

misattribution.heading: Genuine — but often muddled
misattribution.intro: Unlike most quotes pinned on a famous name, this one is really Tutu’s. The wrinkles here are about wording drift and confusion with a similar quote, not authorship.

items.why: The line circulates in several forms — singular “situation” vs plural “situations,” “his foot” vs “its foot” — but all trace to the same passage quoted in Brown’s 1984 book.
A near-identical sentiment — neutrality helping the oppressor — comes from Wiesel’s 1986 Nobel Peace Prize acceptance speech. The two are often swapped; Tutu’s version is the earlier one.

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution to Desmond Tutu is correct: the words are documented in print by 1984 in Robert McAfee Brown’s Unexpected News.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Tutu spoke and preached these words during the apartheid era, when many South Africans and outside observers claimed a comfortable neutrality. His point was that in a situation of entrenched injustice, declining to take a side is not impartiality — it is a choice that benefits whoever already holds power.

The elephant-and-mouse image that follows in Brown’s book makes the argument impossible to soften: to the creature being crushed, the bystander’s neutrality is indistinguishable from the elephant’s weight.
